---
title: "A1 exercises — Structure, scale and feedback"
---

The questions follow the [tutorial](index.qmd) and [slides](lec.qmd). Answer
each question before opening its answer.

## Levels of organisation

### 1.1

Arrange from the smallest to the largest level: organ, organism, cell,
organ system, tissue.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
:::

### 1.2

In a multicellular animal, most cells exchange materials directly with:

a. the external environment
b. interstitial fluid
c. blood plasma
d. the gut lumen

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b. Interstitial (extracellular) fluid surrounds the cells; blood, where present,
transports material between exchange organs and the tissues.
:::

### 1.3

The intestinal wall contains all four primary tissue types. For each tissue
type, give its main function in the intestine.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Tissue | Function in the intestine |
| --- | --- |
| Epithelium | Lines the lumen; secretion and absorption |
| Connective tissue | Supports the epithelium and carries blood vessels |
| Smooth muscle | Mixes and moves the contents |
| Nervous tissue | Coordinates secretion and muscle activity |
:::

### 1.4

Put the steps in order for a glucose molecule moving from the gut lumen into
a skeletal-muscle cell:

a. crosses the muscle-cell membrane
b. crosses the apical membrane of the intestinal epithelial cell
c. is carried in the blood
d. crosses the basolateral membrane of the intestinal epithelial cell
e. enters the interstitial fluid around the muscle fibre

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b → d → c → e → a. Glucose in the lumen has not yet been absorbed, because the
lumen is continuous with the outside of the body.
:::

## Surface area, volume and diffusion

### 2.1

Complete the table for cubes with side length $L$.

| $L$ (mm) | Surface area (mm²) | Volume (mm³) | Surface area : volume (mm⁻¹) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | | | |
| 2 | | | |
| 4 | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| $L$ (mm) | Surface area (mm²) | Volume (mm³) | Surface area : volume (mm⁻¹) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 6 | 1 | 6 |
| 2 | 24 | 8 | 3 |
| 4 | 96 | 64 | 1.5 |

The ratio is $6L^2 / L^3 = 6/L$, so each doubling of $L$ halves it.
:::

### 2.2

The time needed for diffusion is proportional to the square of the distance.
By what factor does the diffusion time change when the distance increases
from:

a. 1 µm to 3 µm
b. 0.1 mm to 1 mm
c. 20 µm to 10 µm

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 3² = 9 times longer.
b. 10² = 100 times longer.
c. (1/2)² = 1/4, i.e. four times shorter.
:::

### 2.3

Name three ways in which large animals overcome the low surface-area-to-volume
ratio of a large body.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

1. Folding, branching or subdivision of exchange surfaces increases the area
   (e.g. alveoli, gill lamellae, intestinal villi).
2. Thin exchange barriers shorten the diffusion distance.
3. Bulk flow (ventilation and circulation) moves material over long distances.
:::

## Tissues

### 3.1

Name the primary tissue type that matches each description.

| | Description |
| --- | --- |
| A | One layer of closely packed cells lining a lumen, with little material between the cells |
| B | Widely spaced cells among abundant parallel extracellular fibres |
| C | Long, cylindrical, striated fibres with many nuclei per fibre |
| D | Cells with long processes, surrounded by many smaller supporting cells |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

A: epithelial tissue (simple epithelium). B: connective tissue (dense regular
connective tissue, e.g. tendon). C: muscle tissue (skeletal muscle).
D: nervous tissue (neurons and glial cells).
:::

### 3.2

Complete the table.

| | Skeletal muscle | Cardiac muscle | Smooth muscle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Striated? | | | |
| Cell shape | | | |
| Nuclei per cell | | | |
| Specialised cell junctions | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Skeletal muscle | Cardiac muscle | Smooth muscle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Striated? | Yes | Yes | No |
| Cell shape | Long cylindrical fibres | Branched cells | Spindle-shaped cells |
| Nuclei per cell | Many | One (sometimes two) | One |
| Specialised cell junctions | No | Intercalated discs | Gap junctions in many smooth muscles |
:::

### 3.3

Which type of epithelium best suits each function: simple squamous or
stratified squamous?

a. gas exchange
b. protection against abrasion

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Simple squamous: a single thin layer gives a short diffusion distance.
b. Stratified squamous: several cell layers protect the tissue beneath.
:::

### 3.4

Define the terms *lumen*, *apical surface* and *basal surface*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

- **Lumen:** the inner space of a tube or cavity, such as the gut or a blood vessel.
- **Apical surface:** the side of an epithelial cell that faces the lumen or
  the outside.
- **Basal surface:** the side of an epithelial cell that faces the basement
  membrane and underlying tissue.
:::

### 3.5

A section shows a circular profile with an empty centre. Why is this not
enough to identify it as a blood vessel?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Any tube (such as a duct, gland, gut or vessel) cut in cross-section gives a
ring. An oblique cut through the same tube gives an oval. Identification also
needs the wall structure, its tissue layers and the scale.
:::

## Homeostasis and feedback

### 4.1

Define homeostasis.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Homeostasis is the active maintenance of internal conditions (such as
temperature or the composition of extracellular fluid) within a range
compatible with life, despite external and internal disturbances.
:::

### 4.2

Body temperature in a mammal rises during exercise. Match each item to its
role in the feedback loop: regulated variable, sensor, control centre, effector.

a. sweat glands
b. hypothalamus
c. body temperature
d. thermoreceptors

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. effector; b. control centre; c. regulated variable; d. sensor.
:::

### 4.3

State whether each example is negative or positive feedback.

a. A rise in blood glucose increases insulin secretion, which lowers blood glucose.
b. Uterine contractions increase oxytocin release, which strengthens the contractions.
c. A rise in body temperature increases sweating.
d. Activated clotting factors activate more clotting factors.
e. A fall in blood pressure increases heart rate through the baroreceptor reflex.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Negative. b. Positive. c. Negative. d. Positive. e. Negative.
:::

### 4.4

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. Positive feedback means that the response is good for the animal.
b. In negative feedback, the response reduces the deviation that triggered it.
c. Positive feedback must have a way to stop.
d. A stable internal concentration means that no transport is taking place.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. False. "Positive" refers to the direction of the loop: the response
   amplifies the original change. It says nothing about benefit.
b. True.
c. True. Otherwise the change keeps growing, as in an action potential or
   during birth.
d. False. Inputs and outputs can balance while transport continues.
:::

## Responses, acclimation and adaptation

### 5.1

Classify each example as an acute response, acclimation or evolutionary
adaptation.

a. Ventilation increases within seconds when an animal starts running.
b. A fish kept at a higher temperature for four weeks changes its enzyme levels.
c. A population of fish living in hypoxic water has inherited larger gill surfaces.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Acute response. b. Acclimation. c. Evolutionary adaptation.
:::

### 5.2

What is the difference between *acclimation* and *acclimatisation*?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Both are reversible changes within one individual. Acclimation describes the
response to a change in one condition, usually in the laboratory.
Acclimatisation describes the response to changes in the natural environment.
:::

### 5.3

Complete the table comparing oxygen delivery to the tissues.

| | Insect | Mammal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Respiratory medium | | |
| Exchange surface | | |
| Route from exchange surface to the tissue cells | | |
| Role of the circulatory system in O₂ transport | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Insect | Mammal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Respiratory medium | Air | Air |
| Exchange surface | Tracheoles, the fine endings of the tracheae, at the tissues | Alveoli in the lungs |
| Route from exchange surface to the tissue cells | Air-filled tracheae branch directly to the tissues | Blood carries O₂, mostly bound to haemoglobin, from lungs to tissues |
| Role of the circulatory system in O₂ transport | Small | Essential |
:::

## Explore: Diffusion limits body size {#explore-a1-scaling}

The demo shows a ball (or flat sheet) of tissue in air-saturated water that
gets O₂ only by diffusion from its surface. Colour shows the O₂ level and the
readouts give A/V, the diffusion time to the centre, the largest size that
diffusion can supply and the O₂ at the centre. Use the radius and O₂-use
sliders, or the preset buttons.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="a1-scaling"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/a1-scaling.js"></script>
```

### E1

Press **Reset** (sphere, radius 0.50 mm, O₂ use 0.20 mL g⁻¹ h⁻¹). Read off:

a. A/V
b. the diffusion time to the centre
c. the O₂ at the centre, as % of the surface value

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 6.00 mm⁻¹ (= 3/r for a sphere).
b. About 62 s ($t \approx x^2/2D$ with $x$ = 0.5 mm and $D$ = 2 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹).
c. 81 %. Every cell gets O₂.
:::

### E2

From Reset, drag the radius up to 1.0 mm.

a. By what factor has A/V changed?
b. By what factor has the diffusion time to the centre changed?
c. What does the readout give as the largest radius that diffusion alone can
   supply?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. It halves, from 6.00 to 3.00 mm⁻¹ (A/V ∝ 1/r).
b. It increases four times, from about 62 s to 250 s (shown as 4 min),
   because diffusion time ∝ r².
c. 1.14 mm. Above this radius an anoxic core appears; at 1.0 mm the centre
   still has about 23 % O₂.
:::

### E3

Press **5 mm ball**. What percentage of the tissue gets no O₂?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

About 64 %. The radius is more than four times the largest radius (1.14 mm)
that diffusion can supply, so most of the volume is anoxic.
:::

### E4

Press **Mouse tissue** (radius 0.50 mm, O₂ use 2.5 mL g⁻¹ h⁻¹, about 12 times
the Reset value).

a. What is now the largest radius that diffusion can supply?
b. Which statement explains the change? (i) the largest radius falls in
   proportion to the O₂ use; (ii) the largest radius falls in proportion to
   the square root of the O₂ use; (iii) the largest radius does not depend
   on the O₂ use.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 323 µm (0.32 mm), so the 0.50 mm ball now has an anoxic core (17 % of the
   tissue).
b. (ii). The largest radius is $\sqrt{6DC_0/M}$; 12.5 times the O₂ use gives
   $\sqrt{12.5} \approx 3.5$ times smaller radius (1.14 mm → 0.32 mm). A
   tissue with a mammalian metabolic rate must therefore be supplied over much
   shorter distances, by capillaries.
:::

### E5

Press **Flatworm** (flat sheet, 0.15 mm half-thickness).

a. What is the largest half-thickness that diffusion can supply?
b. Does this limit depend on the length and width of the sheet?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 660 µm (0.66 mm), i.e. a sheet up to about 1.3 mm thick. For a flat sheet
   the limit is $\sqrt{2DC_0/M}$, which is $1/\sqrt{3}$ of the sphere's limit.
b. No. Only the thickness sets the diffusion distance, so a flatworm can be
   several centimetres long and wide as long as it stays thin.
:::

## Explore: Feedback control of body temperature {#explore-a1-feedback}

The demo simulates body temperature under a heat load from exercise (or cold)
between minute 10 and minute 40. The effector response is proportional to the
deviation from the 37 °C set point. Choose the type of loop with the buttons,
set the gain, response delay and disturbance with the sliders, and read the
deviations in the readout.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="a1-feedback"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/a1-feedback.js"></script>
```

### E6

Press **Reset** (negative feedback, gain 0.5, no delay, disturbance
+0.30 °C min⁻¹).

a. What is the deviation from the set point at minute 40?
b. Is the temperature back at 37 ± 0.1 °C at 60 min?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. +0.55 °C. Some deviation remains during the whole exercise period, because
   the effector response is driven by the deviation itself.
b. Yes.
:::

### E7

Keep negative feedback and set the gain to 1.0, then to 2.0 (**Strong, fast**).
Read the deviation at minute 40 each time. What happens to the remaining
error when the gain is doubled?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Gain 1.0: +0.29 °C. Gain 2.0: +0.15 °C. Doubling the gain roughly halves the
remaining error; a stronger response holds the regulated variable closer to
the set point, but never exactly on it.
:::

### E8

Return to **Reset** and press **None**, then **Positive feedback**. For each,
read the deviation at minute 40 and say whether the temperature is back at
37 °C by 60 min.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Loop | Deviation at minute 40 | Back at 37 °C at 60 min? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| None | +4.66 °C | No |
| Positive feedback | +13.00 °C (runs off the top of the plot) | No |

Without feedback the heat load drives a drift of several degrees. With
positive feedback the response amplifies the deviation, so temperature runs
away out of the survivable range and does not return when exercise stops.
:::

### E9

Press **Strong, slow** (gain 2.0, delay 1.5 min). Then lower the gain to 0.5
while keeping the 1.5 min delay.

a. What happens with gain 2.0 and the delay?
b. What is the largest deviation with gain 0.5 and the delay?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. The temperature overshoots the set point and oscillates with growing
   amplitude until it leaves the survivable range: a strong response that
   acts on old information over-corrects.
b. +0.69 °C (compared with +0.55 °C without delay). With a weaker response
   the delay causes only a small overshoot, and temperature returns to 37 °C.
:::

### E10

Press **Cold** (disturbance −0.30 °C min⁻¹). What is the deviation at minute
40, and is the effector cooling or heating the body?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

−0.55 °C, the mirror image of Reset. The effector trace lies below the line:
it is heating (for example shivering), opposing the fall in temperature.
:::

## R and bioinformatics {#r-exercises}

Run the code below in R or RStudio. Only base R is used (no packages), and all
data are typed directly into the code.

### R1. Surface area to volume of cubes

Complete the last line so that R prints the surface-area-to-volume ratio of
each cube, then run the code. What ratio (mm⁻¹) does R give for the 4 mm cube?

```r
L <- c(1, 2, 4, 8)          # side length of each cube (mm)
area   <- 6 * L^2           # surface area (mm^2)
volume <- L^3               # volume (mm^3)
ratio  <- ____ / ____       # surface-area-to-volume ratio (mm^-1)
ratio
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```r
L <- c(1, 2, 4, 8)          # side length of each cube (mm)
area   <- 6 * L^2           # surface area (mm^2)
volume <- L^3               # volume (mm^3)
ratio  <- area / volume     # surface-area-to-volume ratio (mm^-1)
ratio
```

```
[1] 6.00 3.00 1.50 0.75
```

1.5 mm⁻¹. Each doubling of side length halves the ratio (6/L).
:::

### R2. Diffusion time grows with distance squared

Diffusion time is proportional to the square of distance. Run the code. How
many times longer does diffusion over 100 µm take than over 10 µm?

```r
d <- c(1, 10, 100)          # diffusion distance (micrometres)
t_rel <- d^2 / d[1]^2       # diffusion time relative to 1 micrometre
t_rel
t_rel[3] / t_rel[2]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
[1]     1   100 10000
[1] 100
```

100 times longer: ten times the distance gives one hundred times the time.
:::

### R3. Mean and spread of body temperature

The values are invented teaching numbers: eight readings of a resting
person's core temperature (°C). Run the code and report (a) the mean,
(b) the standard deviation rounded to two decimals, and (c) how many
readings lie outside 36.8–37.2 °C.

```r
temp <- c(36.8, 37.1, 36.9, 37.4, 37.0, 36.6, 37.2, 37.0)
mean(temp)
round(sd(temp), 2)
sum(temp < 36.8 | temp > 37.2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
[1] 37
[1] 0.24
[1] 2
```

a. 37 °C. b. 0.24 °C. c. 2 readings (36.6 and 37.4 °C). The variable
fluctuates around the set point rather than being perfectly constant.
:::

### R4. A disturbance and its correction

Invented teaching numbers: body temperature recorded each minute during and
after a short bout of exercise. Complete the subsetting line so that `high`
keeps only the rows with a temperature above 37.5 °C, then run the code.

a. How many readings are above 37.5 °C?
b. At which minute is the temperature highest?

```r
rec <- data.frame(
  minute = 0:9,
  temp   = c(37.0, 37.3, 37.6, 37.8, 37.7, 37.5, 37.3, 37.2, 37.1, 37.0)
)
high <- rec[rec$temp ____ 37.5, ]
high
nrow(high)
rec$minute[which.max(rec$temp)]
plot(rec$minute, rec$temp, type = "b",
     xlab = "Time (min)", ylab = "Body temperature (°C)")
abline(h = 37, lty = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```r
high <- rec[rec$temp > 37.5, ]
```

```
  minute temp
3      2 37.6
4      3 37.8
5      4 37.7
[1] 3
[1] 3
```

a. 3 readings. b. Minute 3. The plot shows the rise and the return towards
the dashed 37 °C line, as expected when negative feedback opposes a deviation.
:::

### R5. A log–log slope with `lm`

For cubes, area grows more slowly than volume. Fit a straight line to
log₁₀(area) against log₁₀(volume). What is the slope (rounded to three
decimals)?

a. 0.333  b. 0.667  c. 1.000  d. 1.500

```r
L <- c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16)
area   <- 6 * L^2
volume <- L^3
fit <- lm(log10(area) ~ log10(volume))
round(coef(fit), 3)
plot(log10(volume), log10(area))
abline(fit)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
  (Intercept) log10(volume) 
        0.778         0.667 
```

b. 0.667, that is 2/3: area ∝ volume^(2/3). The intercept 0.778 is
log₁₀(6). A slope below 1 on a log–log plot means the surface available per
unit volume falls as size increases.
:::

### R6. Glycine in collagen (bioinformatics)

Collagen, the main fibrous protein of connective-tissue matrix, has a repeating
Gly–X–Y pattern. The string below is residues 181–240 of human collagen
alpha-1(I), copied from UniProt
[P02452](https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P02452.fasta) (one letter per
amino acid; G = glycine). Run the code.

a. What fraction of the residues is glycine (three decimals)?
b. Are all spacings between consecutive glycines equal to 3 (yes/no)?

```r
col1 <- "MGPSGPRGLPGPPGAPGPQGFQGPPGEPGEPGASGPMGPRGPPGPPGKNGDDGEAGKPGR"
aa <- strsplit(col1, "")[[1]]   # split into single letters
length(aa)
sum(aa == "G")
round(mean(aa == "G"), 3)
g_pos <- gregexpr("G", col1)[[1]]   # positions of each G
diff(as.vector(g_pos))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
[1] 60
[1] 20
[1] 0.333
 [1] 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3
```

a. 0.333 (20 of 60). b. Yes: glycine is every third residue. The small
glycine fits in the centre of the collagen triple helix, which is why a
regular sequence pattern underlies the strength of tendon and bone matrix.
:::
